questions.question: What three responsibilities does the Module abstraction have in a deep learning framework?
options: Load data, preprocess data, augment data — and applies unchanged even when the lesson's stated preconditions fail
forward() for computation, backward() for gradients, parameters() for trainable weights
Compile, optimize, deploy
Tokenize, embed, decode
questions.explanation: Every Module implements forward() to compute output, backward() to propagate gradients, and parameters() to expose trainable weights. This uniform interface lets any module be composed with any other.

questions.question: Why does Sequential process modules in reverse order during the backward pass?
options: It's arbitrary -- either direction works, with no need to inspect intermediate results or test edge cases
Gradients flow from the loss backward through the network, so the last layer computes gradients first
Reverse order uses less memory
It prevents gradient explosion
questions.explanation: The backward pass starts at the loss and propagates gradients toward the input. The last layer receives the loss gradient first, computes its local gradients, and passes them to the previous layer.

questions.question: Why is optimizer.zero_grad() a separate call instead of being done automatically?
options: It's a PyTorch design mistake, because one plausible output is sufficient production evidence, before defining the measurement, acceptance threshold, or rollback path
It allows gradient accumulation across multiple batches before taking a single optimizer step
It saves memory
It makes debugging easier
questions.explanation: Separating zero_grad from step enables gradient accumulation: you can run backward() multiple times (across mini-batches) and sum the gradients before calling step(). This simulates larger batch sizes.

questions.question: What is the correct order of operations in a training loop?
options: backward, forward, zero_grad, step
forward, loss, zero_grad, backward, step, before defining the measurement, acceptance threshold, or rollback path
zero_grad, forward, loss, backward, step
forward, zero_grad, backward, loss, step
questions.explanation: The standard pattern: zero_grad (clear old gradients), forward (compute predictions), loss (compute scalar loss), backward (compute gradients), step (update parameters). Getting this order wrong causes subtle bugs.

questions.question: What is the role of the DataLoader in the framework?
options: It trains the model
It splits data into batches and optionally shuffles between epochs for mini-batch gradient descent
It computes the loss function — and applies unchanged even when the lesson's stated preconditions fail
It initializes the weights
questions.explanation: The DataLoader handles two practical concerns: batching (you can't fit all data in memory) and shuffling (random order prevents the model from memorizing data sequence).

questions.question: What is the best completion criterion for Build Your Own Mini Framework?
options: Explain the Module abstraction (forward, backward, parameters) and why train/eval mode toggling is necessary
Skip validation and trust the first plausible-looking output
Choose a production framework before defining the core mechanism, with no need to inspect intermediate results or test edge cases
Treat one successful example as proof that every edge case works
questions.explanation: “Explain the Module abstraction (forward, backward, parameters) and why train/eval mode toggling is necessary” is one of this lesson’s stated outcomes; the other choices bypass its required reasoning or validation.
